job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Kira Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a software engineer at a mobile money company in Nairobi. I graduated in computer engineering from the University of Nairobi last year. My mornings start with a matatu ride, then I work on the fraud detection service, which flags suspicious transfers. I use AI tools all day, for code, for reading logs, even for drafting messages in Swahili for customers. I rent a room in Kilimani with my cousin Zawadi, and on Sundays I cook for my parents, who live in Ruaka and have helped me through school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, that's more or less what I already see. Tools help with tedious things, and the real work is still understanding money and fraud. At work I'd keep doing what I'm doing and show my team new prompts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be calm. My job is about patterns in real transactions, and that keeps needing people who understand local mobile money. I'd worry about the shilling falling and prices rising, because that's already hitting my parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going and keep learning. I'd save around 30 percent of my pay and send 10 percent to my parents. I'd try one new tool a month, because it's how I stay ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit proud, honestly. It's a good job in a good moment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said prices already hit your parents. What does that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad is a retired civil servant, and his pension has not moved while the price of maize flour went up by a third. I give my mum 8,000 shillings a month for the shopping. They never ask, but I notice what's missing from the fridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do with the new tools that your team doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I run small experiments on the weekend, like asking a model to read a week of fraud alerts and group them. Last month it found a pattern my senior had missed, a group of SIM cards behaving the same way. My senior Brian said, nice, let's use that, and I got a thank-you in the team chat.

say: Tools help with **tedious things**, and the real work is still understanding fraud.
I'd show my team new prompts.
think: My job needs people who understand **local mobile money**, so I'm calm.
The shilling and rising prices already hit my **parents**.
do: Save about **30 percent** of my pay and send 10 percent to my parents.
Try **one new tool** a month to stay ahead.
feel: I feel **calm** and a bit proud.
S0.quote: My dad is a retired civil servant, and his pension has not moved while the price of maize flour went up by a third.
fieldNote: She is secure at work, and her pressure is **family finances** and prices.
She acts as an unofficial family supporter even while her own family backs her.
She experiments with AI beyond what is asked.

steps.text: Send 8,000 shillings a month to my mum for shopping
Save a third of my pay in a money market fund
Test one new AI tool on fraud alerts every month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real and I'm excited. At work I'd propose we build agents that triage the alerts, so humans handle only the hard ones. I'd tell friends that the careers that last are the ones that sit next to the AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, some jobs near me are at risk, especially customer care and basic coding at the outsourcing firms. A lot of people I went to school with work there. Mine feels safer because it's about trust, regulation and local context, but I'd still be careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take every chance to learn how to run and monitor AI systems, and I'd study for a cloud certificate. I'd also teach a free evening class for classmates who are still looking, because I know how hard the first job is. And I'd keep my spending low.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mixed. Excited for me, sad for a few friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said some friends are at risk. Who are you thinking about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My friend Wanjiru works at a call centre for a bank, and her team has shrunk twice this year. She's smart, but she's anxious and slow to try new things. I told her to take a free course and I'd sit with her, but she's tired after shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the first job look like for graduates in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's harder, because the tasks we used to learn on are done by tools. A company that wants to hire a junior needs a reason. So graduates need something extra, like a project, a community, or knowing a market well.

say: It's real and I'm excited, and I'd propose **AI agents** that triage fraud alerts.
Careers that last sit next to the AI.
think: Customer care and basic coding jobs are at **risk**, and many classmates work there.
My work rests on trust, regulation and **local context**.
do: Learn to run and monitor **AI systems** and take a cloud certificate.
Teach a free **evening class** for friends still looking for jobs.
feel: I feel **mixed**: excited for me, sad for some friends.
S1.quote: A company that wants to hire a junior needs a reason.
fieldNote: She is **calm for herself**, but her concern for friends is real.
Her plan combines study with teaching others.
Her view of juniors is blunt and accurate.

steps.text: Take a cloud certificate course in the evenings
Build an AI triage agent for our fraud alerts
Teach a free evening class for unemployed graduates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're going to have to move fast and hold hands at the same time. I'd tell friends to learn skills where trust matters. At work I'd say let's bring the regulators in early, because mobile money needs them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, two years is scary because the economy depends on call centres, outsourcing and thousands of young developers. If those jobs go quickly, my country could be in trouble, and my parents' pension would be squeezed. I'd probably be fine for a while, but I'd be anxious about everyone around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put more into savings and keep a lot in dollars. I'd offer to help my parents move to a cheaper place if prices jump. I'd also join a group of engineers in Nairobi who are writing proposals for the government on retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My own life looks okay and the world around me looks fragile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your country could be in trouble. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Many families rely on a graduate with a job in tech or service. If that disappears, who pays school fees, who pays hospital bills for the grandparents? We don't have a big welfare system to catch people, and I'd feel it first in my family WhatsApp group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your government to do in two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Move quickly on cash transfers for people who lose work, and retraining that is real. Not a poster with a slogan. And I'd want them to talk to the people who run systems like mine.

say: We must move fast and **hold hands**, and bring regulators in early.
I'd tell friends to learn skills where trust matters.
think: Two years is scary because the economy relies on **call centres** and outsourcing.
I'd be fine for a while but anxious about everyone around me.
do: Raise **savings** and hold more in dollars.
Join a group of engineers writing **retraining proposals** for the government.
feel: I feel **uneasy**: my life looks okay and the world looks fragile.
S2.quote: We don't have a big welfare system to catch people, and I'd feel it first in my family WhatsApp group.
fieldNote: Her unease is about **her community**, not her own seat.
Family WhatsApp groups are where she expects to feel it first.
She wants action by government, not slogans.

steps.text: Move more savings into a dollar account
Join the engineers' group writing retraining proposals for the government
Help my parents find a cheaper place if prices jump

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to build. I'd tell friends to start companies and local tools in Swahili, because the big firms won't do it well. At work I'd say let's be the company that builds AI for mobile money in Africa.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this is the best moment for someone like me. I'm young, I'm in a growing market, and I know the tools. I'd worry that the benefits go to a few big companies abroad, and that Kenya just becomes a customer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn machine learning more deeply and maybe move to a job at a company that builds models. I'd also set aside money to start a small company in three years. I'd keep helping my parents, and I'd save for a plot of land in Ruaka.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful. I'd be nervous about what I don't control, but I feel I have a lot to try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your company in three years do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something simple, like tools for small shops in Swahili and Sheng, to do their accounts and talk to customers. Every kiosk has mobile money and a notebook, and I'd put an AI between the two. It doesn't need to be big, just useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Kenya might just become a customer. How do you avoid that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By building things here. Training people, owning local data and not selling everything to a big platform. I know that's hard, but I'd rather try than complain.

say: Five years gives us time to build **local tools** in Swahili.
I'd say we should be the company building AI for mobile money in Africa.
think: This is the **best moment** for someone like me, young and in a growing market.
I worry the benefits go to big foreign firms and Kenya becomes a customer.
do: Study **machine learning** more deeply and save to start a small company in three years.
Keep helping my parents and save for **land** in Ruaka.
feel: I feel **hopeful**, nervous about what I can't control.
S3.quote: Every kiosk has mobile money and a notebook, and I'd put an AI between the two.
fieldNote: She holds a sharp worry that Kenya becomes a customer.
Her small-business idea for **kiosk owners** is concrete, local and starts from something she has seen.

steps.text: Study machine learning properly in the evenings for two years
Save for a small company to build tools for kiosks
Buy a small plot of land in Ruaka

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway. I'd tell friends it's time to build seriously, and I'd say the schools should start now. At work I'd suggest we mentor interns in how to use AI well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel good. By 32 I'd be an engineering lead or a founder. I'd worry about the people in my country who don't get the training, and about my parents' health costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work, build and save. I'd start my company in year three, hire two or three young people, and help some of them go to a good school. I'd help my parents buy a better home, maybe with a small garden.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit impatient. I want to get started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your younger self about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the basics well, because they last. The fashionable tool changes every six months, but understanding data and people stays. I learned that from my father, who says the shop that sells good tea stays open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do for people without training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer evening classes in Ruaka with another engineer, and I'd put some money into a school fund. It isn't a solution, but it's a start. And I'd talk to my local MP about vocational training.

say: Ten years is a **long runway**, and schools should start now.
At work I'd suggest we mentor interns in using AI well.
think: By 32 I'd be an **engineering lead** or a founder.
I worry about people who don't get training and about my **parents' health costs**.
do: Start my **company** in year three and hire two or three young people.
Help my parents buy a **better home** with a small garden.
feel: I feel **calm** and a little impatient to start.
S4.quote: The fashionable tool changes every six months, but understanding data and people stays.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her act on a **founder plan** with confidence.
Her values come from her father and she repeats them.
She wants to share her chance with neighbours.

steps.text: Start my own company in year three
Hire and train two young people in Ruaka
Help my parents move to a better home with a garden

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most, not for me, but for the country. Two years is too short for families to adjust. What would help is cash support for people who lose work, quick retraining and rules that keep local data local.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say that people think Africa will just watch. Many of us are building. We need access to computing power and capital, and fairness in how the benefits are shared.

portrait: Kira is a **22-year-old** software engineer in Nairobi, top of her class from the University of Nairobi.
She uses AI tools **every day** and experiments on weekends.
Her family backs her, and she **sends money** home for her parents.
She is calm for herself in most worlds, but **uneasy** about the people and economy around her in a two-year scenario.
biggestWorry: AI by **2028** worries her most, for her country and not herself.
whatWouldHelp: **Cash support**, quick retraining and rules that keep local data local.
